## Introduction

In my R post I looked at body mass and flipper length. Here I use Python on
the same dataset to ask a different question: Is a penguin's bill length
related to its bill depth? The answer turns out to depend on whether you
look at all penguins together or one species at a time.

**Data:** [Palmer Penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/),
Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. The data ship inside the `palmerpenguins`
Python package, so nothing is downloaded when this page is built. The data are
released under the [CC0 licence](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/).

Citation: Horst AM, Hill AP, Gorman KB (2020). *palmerpenguins: Palmer
Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data.* <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3960218>.
The measurements were collected by Gorman KB, Williams TD, Fraser WR (2014),
*PLoS ONE* 9(3): e90081.

## Looking at the data

```{python}
#| label: load-data
penguins = load_penguins()
print(penguins.shape)
penguins.head()
```

Some birds have missing measurements. I count them per column before deciding
what to do.

```{python}
#| label: missing-values
penguins.isna().sum()
```

```{python}
#| label: clean-data
bill_cols = ["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"]
penguins_clean = penguins.dropna(subset=bill_cols)

n_dropped = len(penguins) - len(penguins_clean)
```

I dropped `{python} n_dropped` birds that lacked a bill measurement, leaving
`{python} len(penguins_clean)` penguins.

## Bill size by species

```{python}
#| label: tbl-species-means
#| tbl-cap: "Mean bill length and depth (mm) by species."
penguins_clean.groupby("species")[bill_cols].mean().round(1)
```

## Pooled trend versus within-species trend

First, the correlation across all penguins together. Then, the correlation
inside each species.

```{python}
#| label: correlations
overall_r = penguins_clean["bill_length_mm"].corr(penguins_clean["bill_depth_mm"])

within_r = (
    penguins_clean.groupby("species")[bill_cols]
    .apply(lambda g: g["bill_length_mm"].corr(g["bill_depth_mm"]))
    .rename("correlation")
)

print(f"All penguins pooled: r = {overall_r:.2f}")
within_r.round(2).to_frame()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bill-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Bill length against bill depth. Left: all penguins with one pooled trend line. Right: the same points with one trend line per species."
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5), sharex=True, sharey=True)

x_all = penguins_clean["bill_length_mm"]
y_all = penguins_clean["bill_depth_mm"]

ax1.scatter(x_all, y_all, alpha=0.6, color="grey")
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x_all, y_all, 1)
xs = np.linspace(x_all.min(), x_all.max(), 100)
ax1.plot(xs, slope * xs + intercept, color="black")
ax1.set_title("All penguins pooled")

for name, group in penguins_clean.groupby("species"):
    ax2.scatter(group["bill_length_mm"], group["bill_depth_mm"], label=name, alpha=0.6)
    s, i = np.polyfit(group["bill_length_mm"], group["bill_depth_mm"], 1)
    xs = np.linspace(group["bill_length_mm"].min(), group["bill_length_mm"].max(), 50)
    ax2.plot(xs, s * xs + i)
ax2.set_title("Split by species")
ax2.legend(title="Species")

for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)")
ax1.set_ylabel("Bill depth (mm)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## What I found

- Across all penguins pooled, bill length and bill depth are negatively
  correlated (r = `{python} round(overall_r, 2)`). @fig-bill-scatter shows this
  in the left panel.
- Within each species the relationship reverses. The correlations range from
  `{python} round(within_r.min(), 2)` to `{python} round(within_r.max(), 2)`,
  all positive.
- The pooled trend is misleading because species differ in both measurements:
  Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills, and Adelie penguins have short
  but deep ones. This is an example of Simpson's paradox, and it is a good
  reason to look at group structure before trusting a pooled correlation.
